papers.title: Reconstruction of extreme temperature events in medieval Poland (1001–1500 CE) from documentary evidence
papers.authors: Akbari Moghaddam Sani, S., Przybylak, R., Oliński, P.
papers.abstract: Abstract Understanding the frequency, intensity, and societal impacts of extreme weather is essential for reconstructing past climate variability, yet systematic documentary-based reconstructions remain remarkably limited for medieval Poland. To address this gap in pre-instrumental data, this study reconstructs extreme temperature-related weather and climate events in Poland between 1001 and 1500 CE utilizing historical documentary evidence. A total of 299 extreme events were verified and synthesized from 452 primary weather notes. To mitigate duplication, overlapping accounts of the same anomaly were cross-referenced and merged. Validated events were categorized into severe frost; cold waves; river, lake, and sea ice events; snow and snowstorms; and heat and warm waves, with each classified by intensity, duration, and source reliability. The findings reveal a clear dominance of cold-related extremes, particularly severe frost and cold waves. A significant increase in the frequency and clustering of these events is observed during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, peaking specifically in the 1440s and 1450s. This pattern aligns with the broader Central European transition into the early phase of the Little Ice Age. Spatial analysis indicates a concentration of recorded events in the Baltic Coast, Pomerania, and Silesia, though this partly reflects uneven source preservation in prominent historical economic centers. Furthermore, cold extremes heavily disrupted transportation and caused environmental stress, whereas heat waves were strongly associated with agricultural damage. By integrating documentary evidence with quantitative analysis, this database provides crucial insights into historical climate variability and climate-society interactions.

papers.title: Complex lake effects structure bryophyte communities across spatial scales around Lake Superior, Canada
papers.authors: Varina E. Crisfield, D. Holt-Schmitt, Valentinà Buttò, Nicole J. Fenton
papers.abstract: Studies have found that large lakes significantly modify regional climates, an influence known as the “lake effect”. Large lakes may provide biodiversity refugia in a changing climate owing to the lake effect, but the impacts of lake effects on biodiversity remain poorly documented. We sought to quantify the influence of the lake effect on bryophyte communities in the vicinity of Lake Superior, and to disentangle the lake effect from processes occurring at larger (regional) and smaller (forest stand) scales. We sampled bryophyte communities on three substrates (trees, rocks, and logs) across 54 sites on and near the northern and eastern shores of Lake Superior. We combined community data with climate and forest data to determine the influence of variables at each of three spatial scales—micro (forest attributes), meso (lake effect), and macro (regional climatic norms)—on community composition and richness. The lake effect structured community composition, along with regional climate norms and forest characteristics. The lake effect was divided into three orthogonal axes. Notably, each of these axes included a distinct component of the moisture environment—precipitation, relative humidity, and vapour pressure deficit—and our results suggest that these components have divergent effects on bryophyte communities. The lake effect had no significant influence on species richness. Lake Superior induces biotically important climatic heterogeneity that structures bryophyte communities across the study region. The near-lake environment may be an important thermal and hydrologic refuge for bryophytes in a warming, drying climate.

papers.title: Declining environmental predictability erodes reproduction in a tropical seabird
papers.authors: Santiago Ortega, Cristina Rodríguez, Ayumi Mizuno et al.
papers.abstract: Seasonal breeders often depend on predictable resource pulses, yet climate change may alter reliability without shifting average timing. Here, using satellite chlorophyll records and two decades of individual breeding data for a tropical seabird, we show that weakened breeding synchrony and declining and less consistent reproductive success were associated with increasingly variable bloom timing without a consistent directional shift. Focusing on average timing alone could mean that climate impacts on species are overlooked. The authors show that, for a tropical seabird model species, winter–spring phytoplankton blooms kept a stable mean timing but became more variable between years. Breeding synchrony weakened and reproductive success declined and became less consistent over the same two decades.

papers.title: Short-term shallow landslide early warning framework integrating radar-based precipitation forecasts and a physically based slope stability model in Taiwan
papers.authors: Jui-Yi Ho, Chung-Yi Lin, Che-Hsin Liu et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Taiwan is prone to hillslope disasters in mountain areas because of its special topographical, geological, and hydrological conditions. During typhoons and rainstorms, severe shallow landslides frequently occur. To mitigate the impact of shallow landslides, not only the structural measures are necessary, but also adequate warning systems and contingency measures must be executed. Hence, precise precipitation forecasts and landslide prediction are the most important measures in practice. To account for inherent weather uncertainties precipitation forecasts based on quantitative precipitation forecast model with radar data assimilation method and ensemble mean prediction were adopted in this study instead of using a single model output. The SIMTOP model based on infinite-slope model and TOPMODEL was developed. In considering detail topographic characteristics of the subcatchments, the proposed model can estimate the variation of saturated water level during rainstorms, and then link with the slope instability analysis to clarify whether shallow landslides would occur in the subcatchment. Two area vulnerable to landslide in Taiwan were collected to test the applicability of the model for landslide prediction. Six typhoons events were used to verify the applicability of the proposed model. Four indexes including the probability of detection (POD), false alarm ratio (FAR), threat score (TS), and accuracy (ACC) were adopted to assess the performance of two kinds of very short-term rainfall forecasts with SIMTOP model. The results indicate that quantitative precipitation forecast model with radar data assimilation with SIMTOP model was better than ensemble rainfall forecasts with SIMTOP model. It is promising to apply the proposed model for landslide early warnings to reduce the magnitude of the loss of lives and properties.

papers.title: Landslide susceptibility mapping through the integration of pixel and slope unit analyses: a case study in El Salvador, Central America
papers.authors: Christian Conoscenti, Abel Alexei Argueta-Platero, Liborio Barbera et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Landslide susceptibility mapping is commonly performed using either pixel-based or slope-unit (SU)-based approaches, each characterised by specific advantages and limitations. In this study, SU-level information is incorporated directly into a pixel-based modelling framework to assess whether this integration improves model performance and the spatial organisation of susceptibility maps. The analysis focuses on the northern sector of the Ilopango Caldera (El Salvador), where shallow landslides were triggered by Tropical Storms Amanda and Cristobal in 2020. A 2 m resolution LiDAR-derived DEM was used to derive pixel-scale terrain predictors and to delineate slope units through hydrological analysis. Two configurations were tested: a Baseline model based solely on pixel-scale variables and an Enhanced model including SU-based morphometric summaries and lithological proportions. Both configurations were implemented using Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) and Random Forest (RF) and evaluated through repeated spatial cross-validation. The Enhanced models systematically outperformed the Baseline models. Mean AUC increased from 0.927 to 0.942 for MARS and from 0.923 to 0.949 for RF. In addition to the improvement in predictive performance, the Enhanced configuration produced maps characterised by higher spatial autocorrelation, measured using Global Moran’s I, and reduced local fragmentation, while maintaining variability within individual slope units. These results indicate that integrating SU-derived descriptors during model calibration strengthens the predictive capability of pixel-based models and improves the spatial consistency of the resulting maps, without sacrificing pixel-scale detail.

papers.title: Short-term shallow landslide early warning framework integrating radar-based precipitation forecasts and a physically based slope stability model in Taiwan
papers.authors: Authors not listed
papers.abstract: Shallow landslides are among the most frequent rainfall-induced hazards in Taiwan’s mountainous regions, particularly during typhoon events when rainfall intensity changes rapidly over short periods. Reliable very short-term rainfall forecast is therefore essential for enhancing near-real-time landslide early warning. This study develops an integrated framework that couples two quantitative precipitation forecast (QPF) approaches—radar data assimilation and ensemble mean forecasts—with the physically based SIMTOP slope stability model. Six typhoon events associated with documented shallow landslides were selected to evaluate the forecasting skill and warning performance of the combined system. The rainfall forecast assessment showed that both QPF methods performed reasonably well for 1–3 h lead times but deteriorated beyond 4 h. Radar-assimilated forecasts consistently provided more accurate representations of rainfall evolution than ensemble means, particularly in capturing peak intensities. When incorporated into SIMTOP, the radar-based QPF produced stronger short-term landslide predictions, achieving POD, FAR, TS, and ACC values of 0.813, 0.480, 0.464, and 0.979, respectively, for 1–4 h forecasts. Performance declined at 5–6 h due to increasing uncertainty, whereas the ensemble mean forecasts displayed generally weaker skill across all lead times. Overall, the results indicate that integrating radar-enhanced precipitation forecasts with a physically based slope stability model can substantially improve the timeliness and reliability of shallow landslide warnings under typhoon rainfall. The proposed framework provides a practical tool for supporting rapid emergency response and for strengthening disaster risk reduction efforts in landslide-prone mountain areas.

papers.title: Geo-social media beyond Twitter: Comparing retrieval strategies for Reddit, TikTok, Telegram, Mastodon, and Bluesky during the 2024 Central European floods
papers.authors: Shaily Raju Gandhi, Marco Badici, David Hanny et al.
papers.abstract: Social media can provide timely information during floods, but cross-platform keyword retrieval remains challenging because search interfaces and access conditions differ. This study retrospectively compared English- and German-language posts retrieved from Bluesky, Mastodon, Reddit, TikTok and Telegram during the September 2024 Central European floods. Two strategies - phrase-based queries (Test 1) and root-based, stem-like queries (Test 2) - were applied using equivalent keyword sets adapted to each platform’s constraints. Performance was evaluated in terms of retrieval volume, duplication, disaster relatedness, relevance and geoparsed location references. Spatial patterns were analysed through H3 aggregation and spatial autocorrelation and validated against a satellite-derived flood mask. Bluesky and TikTok yielded the largest volumes (11,232 versus 49,386 posts and 9718 versus 25,560 posts, respectively, for Tests 1 and 2), whereas Reddit (246 versus 249) and Telegram (85 versus 83) had substantially fewer posts. Root-based queries substantially increased retrieval volume on Bluesky, Mastodon and TikTok, but phrase-based queries produced a higher proportion of relevant content. About one third of geocoded related-and-relevant posts (33.1% and 34.4%) were geoparsed to the United States, showing that global retrieval captures international discourse alongside local observations; spatial analyses were therefore restricted to Central Europe. At H3 Level 4, 83.81% of occupied cells under Test 1 and 81.82% under Test 2 intersected the flood mask, exceeding the 67.73% spatial baseline. Cells containing posts from multiple platforms represented 40.00% and 36.36% of the respective spatial footprints. Multi-platform integration increased overall spatial completeness and reduced the likelihood of platform-specific blind spots.

papers.title: Effects of high elevation wildfires on peak snow water equivalent in California's Sierra Nevada headwater regions
papers.authors: Xiaoyu Liang, Yufang Jin, Kyle  R. Knipper et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Increases in high‐elevation wildfires in California’s Sierra Nevada region (SNR) have raised concerns about potential impacts on snowpack, a major source for the state’s water supply. Quantifying fire-induced changes in snow storage remains challenging in mountainous regions with complex topography and large climatic and ecological gradients, due to limited field observations and process models. This study leveraged high-resolution Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) lidar surveys (2023-2024) to assess the impacts of 2020-2021 wildfires on peak snow water equivalent (SWE) across six SNR watersheds. We assembled >32,000 matched burned-unburned 50-m pixel pairs with similar pre-fire environmental conditions and assessed how changes in peak SWE (ΔpeakSWE: burned - unburned) varied with burn severity, pre-fire forest structure, meteorological variables, and terrain above the snowline. Across matched pairs, post-fire peak SWE differences varied in both magnitude and direction, depending on yearly weather (e.g., wet vs. normal year) and local environmental setting. The largest positive burned–unburned difference occurred in dense forests with ≥75% canopy loss at intermediate elevations in 2023, where burned areas had 13.0 cm higher peak SWE on average (12% relative to the matched unburned mean of 105.1 cm); this difference was substantially smaller in 2024. The spatially cross-validated extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) machine learning model showed terrain provided the strongest predictive information, followed by vegetation structure. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and a shallow decision tree further showed that sites with lower heat exposure, locally lower terrain positions, and intermediate elevations generally were associated with higher peak SWE in burned areas compared to matched unburned areas, whereas taller pre-fire canopies and exposed, high-energy terrain were associated with lower peak SWE. These results demonstrate wildfire effects on peak SWE are strongly context dependent and provide an assessment framework for anticipating where high elevation wildfires may increase or reduce mountain snow storage.

papers.title: Land-use input choice and policy-relevant environmental and sustainability indicators: a sensitivity assessment for Brazil
papers.authors: Chiara Colesanti Senni, Justin A. Johnson
papers.abstract: Abstract Global assessments of climate, biodiversity, and ecosystem services rely on projections of land-use change (LUC), typically from integrated assessment models (IAMs) at coarse resolution (25 to 50 km) and downscaled to the 30 to 300 m required by biophysical models. The choice of LUC projection introduces large variation in results, but this variation is rarely assessed. For Brazil, we systematically compare two LUC projections, a regionally calibrated model (Land Use and Cover Change Modelling Environment, LuccME) and a global product (Land-Use Harmonization 2, LUH2), downscaling both to 300 m with the Spatial Economic Allocation Landscape Simulator (SEALS) and computing five sustainability indicators (biomass carbon, biodiversity intactness, water yield, Forest Code compliance, and a diffuse-nitrogen index). The differences are large, from −37 to +45 % for biomass carbon, −20 to +23 % for water yield, −76 to +12 % for the diffuse-nitrogen index, and −0.27 to +0.17 in mean species abundance. The choice between the two projections also flips the Forest Code compliance call on 9 to 26 % of Brazil's land grid cells, and several biome-level shifts reverse sign under an alternative class correspondence, a sensitivity we quantify. Differences of this size could materially affect sustainability analyses, including REDD+ accounting, where a shifted carbon baseline could change results-based payments, as well as biodiversity assessment and nature-related financial-risk analysis.

papers.authors: Sarah K. Newcomb, Robert Van Kirk, Sarah E. Godsey, Otto Lang
papers.abstract: Abstract Globally, mountainous headwaters are projected to experience less precipitation falling as snow. Changes in snowmelt rate and timing may affect streamflow generation by shifting the alignment of energy and water inputs which control the proportion of precipitation lost to the atmosphere, or evapotranspiration (ET) efficiency. Since changes in ET efficiency may make streamflow harder to predict in seasonally snow-covered watersheds, in this study, we investigate the impact of precipitation phase on ET efficiency in eight watersheds across the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. Across all watersheds, mixed effects modeling shows that more available water goes to ET in low snow-fraction years. However, ET responses to snow conditions are locally moderated: groundwater-dominated watersheds are less responsive in the short term but retain a stronger memory of the previous year's conditions. papers.authors: Zejiang Yin, Zhang Lei, Song Yang et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Subtropical East Asia, among the world's most densely populated regions and a major agricultural region, has experienced pronounced early-spring drying since the 1980s, posing growing risks to water resources and agriculture. However, the relative contributions of external forcing and internal variability to the drying trend, as well as the associated dynamic and thermodynamic processes, remain unclear. The circulation analogues-based dynamic adjustment reveals that atmospheric circulation changes explain approximately 108% of the observed drying trend, which were largely driven by internal variability. These circulation changes are closely linked to a positive-to-negative phase transition of the Interdecadal Pacific Variability (IPV), which can suppress precipitation by weakening the Northwest Pacific anticyclone and inducing anomalous subsidence over subtropical East Asia. The IPV also modulates near-term precipitation projections. Based on the projected IPV inferred from ensemble members that realistically capture the historical IPV, we identify a likely reversal toward wetter conditions in the near future.

papers.title: Identifying the indirect cost of work in high-heat conditions
papers.authors: Steven C. Sherwood, Timothy L. Neal, Ollie Jay
papers.abstract: Abstract The impact of excess heat on labor productivity and/or labor supply are a key contributor to the total economic impact of climate change on the macroeconomy. Empirically, workers typically exceed international safety standard work hours under hot conditions, suggesting they are incurring indirect costs in order to reduce production losses. Here we take a simple agent-based perspective on this question, supposing that workers and their employers make this tradeoff optimally. Based on this and a few other simple assumptions we infer workplace heat impacts on human health and well being that may be an appreciable fraction of economic losses. This implies that current studies underestimate the true costs of workplace heat in the present, and especially, future climates.

papers.title: Spatially compounding climate extremes and environmental risk: cross-regional synchrony, spatial buffering loss, and systemic consequences
papers.authors: 朱爱辉, Dayun Zhu
papers.abstract: Abstract Spatially compounding climate extremes are increasingly recognized as a source of climate-related risk, and their risk significance depends on how synchrony affects connected systems. The critical transition occurs when cross-regional synchrony reduces support from places that would otherwise buffer one another through substitution, reserve capacity, mutual assistance or recovery support—a condition we term spatial buffering loss. This Topical Review synthesizes empirical and methodological evidence to examine how synchrony is generated, when it translates into functional loss, and what is required to assess that transition. Food production, water allocation and firefighting cooperation provide complementary settings for examining substitution, reserve and assistance functions, while the synthesis distinguishes joint exposure from support available to recipients. Atmospheric circulation, persistent weather patterns, land–atmosphere feedbacks and hydrological connectivity can organize synchrony; functional evidence determines whether that synchrony reduces compensating support and produces systemic consequences. Accordingly, credible assessment must connect event topology and joint-tail behaviour with functional exposure, an explicit compensating relation and a counterfactual estimate of support that would otherwise have remained available. By linking event organization to recipient support, the synthesis provides a functional basis for assessing spatial buffering loss across connected systems. This perspective connects the evidence to decisions about supplier diversification, reserve operation and mutual assistance.

papers.title: Who collects, who purchases? Land ownership and biomass acquisition in LMICs
papers.authors: Dim, J., Lopez Soto, D., Balasubramanya, S., Kumar, P.
papers.abstract: Abstract This study examines the relationship between agricultural land ownership and household fuel use behavior in low- and middle-income countries. Using harmonized household survey data from 11 countries and pooled regressions with country fixed effects, the analysis compares land-owning and landless households across three dimensions of fuel behavior: firewood collection, firewood purchase, and firewood use as the main cooking fuel. The results show that land-owning households are more likely to collect firewood, less likely to purchase it, and more likely to rely on firewood as their primary cooking fuel. These findings persist after controlling for wealth, urban residence, electricity access, and household composition. Interaction models indicate that the land–collection relationship is stable across varying contexts, while the land–purchase relationship is weaker among urban and wealthier households, suggesting that land ownership may shift households from self-collection to purchase rather than out of biomass use altogether. Time-use regressions further show that land-owning households spend more time gathering and preparing fuel, indicating that access to biomass through land lowers cash expenditures but not labor costs. Overall, the findings suggest that land ownership is an important structural determinant of household fuel use behavior and that cooking transitions may depend not only on income and infrastructure, but also on access to biomass resources through land. The analysis demonstrates that the land–energy nexus deserves greater attention in future household energy research and in policies aimed at accelerating equitable and sustained cooking transitions.

papers.title: Evolving energy-water infrastructure strengthens drought resilience in the U.S. Northeast and Midwest
papers.authors: Hussain H. Bokhari, Charles J Vörösmarty, Stephanie Herbert, Carry Pak
papers.abstract: Abstract Strategies to strengthen regional water security will be essential for navigating a critical 21st-century environmental challenge: securing freshwater supplies against growing demands and increasingly severe climate extremes. This paper assesses the evolution of water security in the historically water-rich U.S. Northeast (NE) and Midwest (MW) to quantify their resilience to severe drought now and in the future. We develop a counterfactual framework that projects sectoral water demands based on socio-economic drivers and deconstructs the benefits of supply- and demand-side adaptations at the regional scale. During the half-century between the historic NE/MW 1960s drought and the 2012-2013 North American drought, rapid socio-economic growth held the potential to push water systems to a breaking point, rendering them unequipped to manage the impact of such severe droughts. However, this study reveals that both regions built resilience through long-term adaptations that averted potential water crises, mitigating otherwise severe summertime water stress (withdrawal-to-available supply) by factors of 2.8 (MW) and 5.6 (NE). While supply-side strategies through reservoir construction and coastal power development played a role, the driving factor has been water demand management, accounting for 83% to 92% of summertime water stress mitigations across the two regions and drought scenarios. These gains were rooted in economic and political incentives to adopt advanced thermoelectric cooling technologies and efficient industrial technologies, together with the regions’ shift from a manufacturing to service economy. Thus, our projections of increased water demand by the mid-21st century highlight a critical reality: future drought resilience will require continued investments in demand-side efficiency gains, such as water-efficient electricity production systems, to keep pace with expected socio-economic trends.

papers.title: Additionality of climate benefits from emission reduction and carbon dioxide removal
papers.authors: Ganey, T., Hain, M., Ridgwell, A., Paytan, A.
papers.abstract: Abstract Carbon dioxide removal (CDR) has been identified as a necessary complement to industrial decarbonization for climate change mitigation. Marine CDR (mCDR) approaches, such as ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) and direct ocean capture (DOC), have received considerable attention for their potential to counteract ocean acidification while simultaneously reducing atmospheric CO 2 . However, most model-based assessments of mCDR efficacy either assume a fixed background atmospheric CO 2 value or adopt an idealized future CO 2 trajectory, thereby excluding impacts of important carbon cycle feedbacks that repartition carbon between the ocean, atmosphere, and biosphere. Here, we use an Earth system model to address three core questions: whether the net CO 2 effect of CDR depends on background emissions; whether CDR technologies deployed simultaneously yield additive CO 2 reductions; and whether there is synergy between the radiative forcing (climate) benefits of CDR and emission reductions. We evaluate permutations of direct air capture, OAE, and DOC, quantifying their individual and combined CO 2 effects under various emissions scenarios. We find that the radiative forcing effects of emissions reductions and CDR are largely additive through time, regardless of background emission scenario or CDR type or scale. Furthermore, any given quantity and type of short-term CDR deployment produces a predictable, proportional and durable reduction in atmospheric CO 2 through time (ΔlnCO 2 ), facilitating comparison between CDR strategies. Finally, we show that CDR efficacy is marginally greater at low background CO 2 , supporting the complementary value of decarbonization and CDR in carbon management portfolios. These findings provide a robust physical basis for the design of integrated carbon management strategies and support pursuit of deep emissions cuts and CDR as synergistic climate levers.

papers.title: Have we already lost it? Geoprivacy in the age of AI, uncertainty, and corporate gatekeeping
papers.authors: Milad Malekzadeh, Jim Thatcher, Grant McKenzie et al.
papers.abstract: Geoprivacy is often framed as a problem of protecting coordinates, masking traces, or managing user consent. This framing is now insufficient. In an era of pervasive datafication, AI-enabled inference, platform dependence, and corporate control over location and mobility data, the central question is no longer whether exact locations can be hidden, but whether meaningful control over location-derived knowledge remains possible at all. This paper asks: have we already lost geoprivacy? We argue that geoprivacy has not disappeared, but its conditions have fundamentally changed. Location data are now continuously produced through everyday digital participation, linked across platforms and modalities, and transformed by machine learning, large language models, and agentic systems into sensitive inferences about identity, behavior, association, vulnerability, and future action. At the same time, risks and protections are unevenly distributed: privacy increasingly functions as socioeconomic, political, and institutional privilege, while marginalized communities, sensitive places, non-human environments, and collective forms of knowledge face heightened exposure and risk. These challenges are intensified by corporate gateke eping, regulatory lag, harmful defaults, limited transparency, and epistemic blind spots within existing geoprivacy norms and directions. We therefore reposition geoprivacy as a socio-technical, legal, institutional, and political problem, not merely a technical one. Looking forward, we outline responsibilities for policymakers, researchers, communities, and industry, including privacy-protective defaults, regulation of spatial inference, public-good data governance, geoprivacy literacy, cyber-threat exercises, and community-controlled infrastructures. Rather than declaring geoprivacy lost, we argue that it must be continually renegotiated as a moving boundary, one that requires GI science to act not only as a technical field, but as a bridge between spatial reasoning, governance, justice, and democratic control over location-based data and futures.

papers.authors: Kyle J. A. Zawada, Emily S. Darling, Stacy D. Jupiter et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Climate change is accelerating the decline of coral reefs, yet some locations may retain conditions that support persistence under future warming. We compiled 45,064 coral field observations from 1960–2025 and 42 climate, biophysical, and human-pressure predictors to train machine-learning ensembles estimating coral cover and community composition in 2020 and 2050. We then used a multi-objective optimization framework to select, within each ecoregion, 30% of the reef area (consistent with the GBF 30x30 target) that jointly maximized current and future coral cover, community composition, spatial cohesion, and model certainty as indicators of climate resilience. Finally, we evaluated our results against three global coral reef habitat layers, including two products from the Allen Coral Atlas (visible reef extent and a coral habitat subset) and a UNEP-WCMC global distribution of coral reefs. The three layers identify between 36,466 to 167,352 km2 of coral reef areas with relatively high projected persistence to survive climate change, spanning 79 to 81 national EEZs and 57 to 60 territories and jurisdictions. These findings show how empirical observations and multivariate machine learning can be combined to map candidate climate-resilient reefs at fine resolution, and reveal their uneven but widespread global distribution. While predictive skill was modest and varied among provinces, our results identify candidate locations with the highest probability of sustaining functioning coral reef futures rather than definitive priorities, and should be combined with local knowledge, national assessments and improved monitoring data to inform conservation policy, finance and management.

papers.abstract: Abstract Earth System Models used to quantify climate-carbon cycle feedbacks and remaining carbon budgets are initialised from pre-industrial land-use conditions, yet the real world has experienced centuries of land-use change. Whether the resulting land-surface state affects the diagnosed feedback parameters-concentration-carbon (β land ) and climate-carbon (γ land )-and the Transient Climate Response to cumulative Emissions (TCRE) remains poorly explored.Here we quantify how different initial land-use states-no land-use, pre-industrial, and present-day-affect carbon cycle feedback parameters in standard 1% CO 2 coupled and biogeochemically coupled simulations using HadCM3LC-Bris. This implies a systematic positive bias of ∼8% in TCRE diagnosed from pre-industrial-initialised experiments, corresponding to ∼40 GtCO 2 for a 1.5 • C carbon budget. At higher forcing, the land-use effect on TCRE diminishes as α differences converge while γ land continues to diverge. Our results highlight a baseline-dependent bias in current CMIP protocol design with direct implications for carbon budget estimates.

papers.authors: Ritodhi Chakraborty, Pasang Yangjee Sherpa, Eric Nost et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract In recent global climatic and environmental reports, Indigenous Knowledges (IK) are recognised as essential to comprehending social-ecological systems and multi-scalar climate-society relationships. However, IK and Indigenous Peoples (IP) continue to be mostly excluded from important and powerful processes such as the UNFCCC and the IPCC reports. In the current (AR7) cycle of the IPCC, it is important to understand whether the last cycle (AR6) meaningfully engaged with IK and IP. Here, we present a multi-tiered bibliometric analysis of the literature cited in the AR6 report (n=46,145 citations), through which we identified citations with abstracts mentioning IK (n=482). Additionally, through exploring this cluster of IK citations, we address enduring questions around disciplinary bias, geographical bias, and academic journal bias. Finally, we categorise IK citations using two indexes of equitable knowledge production. This highlights the different types of relationships (from extractive to co-productive) that guided the cited papers’ research process. Our findings highlight that despite advocacy, promises, and assurances, IK is mostly excluded from the IPCC AR6 report (1.04% of scholarly literature cited). We also call attention to the fact that biophysical sciences, elite journals, and authors from the Global North are dominant in the IK that is included. Finally, we identify some key points of intervention for AR7, which include strategic choices for chapter authors, a focus on Working Group I (climate science), and the inclusion of chapter-scale knowledge justice audits.

papers.authors: Daigneault, A., Sohngen, B., Belair, E., Ellis, P.
papers.abstract: Abstract Filewod (2026 Environ. Res. Lett. 20 114022) Comment questions whether the Global Timber Model (GTM) used in Daigneault et al (2025 Environ. Res. Lett. 20 114022) should be to quantify the carbon leakage from climate-smart forestry (CSF) practices. We share the Comment’s goal of protecting the integrity of forest carbon credits and mitigate climate change, but differ on whether model-based estimates should inform crediting adjustments, particularly while ex-post evidence of recent CSF projects accumulates. We clarify and stand by our study conclusions that our estimates support ex-ante, multi-factor leakage deductions, that forest carbon leakage can vary widely depending on the project type and location, and that carbon leakage is typically lower than harvest leakage. We also acknowledge the strong market assumptions underlying GTM and show that discounting carbon leakage that accrues in the distant future reduces the influence of far off supply responses thereby providing conservative estimates. We acknowledge that ex-ante model intercomparison and robust ex-post analysis can offer a shared path toward more robust and credible leakage accounting.

papers.title: Decoupled ore and scrap trade networks constrain low-carbon metal supply
papers.authors: Tian, X., Mao, Y., Geng, Y., Taylor, D.
papers.abstract: Abstract Global supply chains for critical metals such as aluminium and copper are increasingly exposed to sustainability and geopolitical risks under the pressure of energy transition. In this paper we compare primary (ore) and secondary (scrap) trade networks for the United States, European Union and China using multilayer network analysis. We focus on the years 2010–2023, a period that captures intensified demand for the two metals. Results identify a marked structural decoupling: around 40% of scrap-trading countries do not participate in ore trade. Further, while about 50% of ore trade links overlap with scrap networks, only some 10%–15% of scrap connections overlap with ore trade. Despite strong alignment in trading partners, volumes of scrap and ore trade diverge substantially. The observed differences indicate that the two commodity streams use partly distinct international trading relationships. Major economies may compete for ore suppliers but remain interdependent in scrap trade, revealing a bifurcated system with uneven resilience. Strengthening integration between primary and secondary supply chains is therefore critical for achieving sustainable critical metal supply for the low-carbon energy transition and establishing resource-efficient metal systems.

papers.title: Wealth, homeownership, and land use regulatory changes
papers.authors: Diego Gil, Hugo E. Silva, Kenzo Asahi
papers.abstract: This paper examines patterns of land use regulatory changes in Santiago, Chile, focusing on downzoning (stricter regulations) and upzoning (more flexible regulations), and their associations with sociodemographic factors. We analyze an original georeferenced dataset covering all 34 urban municipalities of Santiago over 20 years, together with 19 semi-structured interviews with key actors. The quantitative analysis suggests that high-income neighborhoods are associated with a greater likelihood of downzoning when homeownership is comparatively low. With our block-level measure of wealth, however, this association is not statistically distinguishable from zero at the sample-average homeownership rate and becomes negative at higher rates. Therefore, in affluent neighborhoods, the significant presence of homeowners is associated with less probability of downzoning. Outside high-income neighborhoods, higher homeownership is instead associated with downzoning. Qualitative evidence points to the growing role of organized residents, with socially connected groups using participatory reforms and informal ties to municipal decision-makers to shape local regulatory debates. This positive association is absent when the analysis is restricted to large-scale zoning changes. The findings contribute to debates between the “growth machine” and “homevoter” theories by suggesting that the relevance of each framework may vary across patterns of social segmentation and local demographic structures.

papers.title: Activity spaces, community resource brokers, and real-time stress and affect: Evidence from the Boston Activity Space and Health Study
papers.authors: Gregory Sharp, Emily C. Walton
papers.abstract: While we know that the places where we live matter for our health and well-being, other spaces in the city we visit during the day—like places where we work, worship, exercise, and buy groceries—also matter. Little work, however, has explored how daily experiences with these routine community institutions and organizations shape our emotional responses. This study uses data from the Boston Activity Space and Health Study (BASHS), a smartphone-based data collection of adults’ GPS locations and ecological momentary assessments, to capture in-the-moment responses to their daily activity space environments for 7 days. We use random effects models to estimate associations between resource broker access and real-time accounts of stress and affect, and whether these relationships are conditional on the utilization of the resource brokers. Our findings suggest that beyond having regular access to community resource brokers, utilizing them on a regular basis is impactful for alleviating momentary emotional and physiological distress. By detailing the unique role of resource brokers, the current study makes substantive and methodological contributions to our understanding of how activity spaces matter for health and well-being.

papers.title: Planning for circular urban metabolism: Intertwining skills and spatial transformation for manufacturing transition in Padua and Venice, Italy
papers.authors: Claudia Faraone, Francesca Gambarotto, Luca Nicoletto, Giulio Pedrini
papers.abstract: The shift from a linear to a circular economic structure needs a new urban metabolism that minimizes waste and the use of raw materials and energy. However, a city’s potential for circularity is contingent upon its manufacturing path-dependency, both from an economic and spatial perspective. The research looks at two Italian industrial areas—Padua and Venice—and proceeds to investigate the recent dynamics of their manufacturing spatial distribution at the “transect” level scale. Using a mixed-method approach that combines morphological-spatial analysis, urban planning assessment, and quantitative labor and waste data, the study investigates how manufacturing industries contribute to circular transitions and how planning policies can support or hinder this process. Findings show that technological manufacturing, supported by technical skills and green jobs, drives circular performance through waste prevention and recycling. Industrial diversification and firm relatedness further enable symbiotic material flows. However, both cities reveal a persistent misalignment between emerging circular dynamics and existing zoning frameworks. While Padua has begun adopting mixed-use zoning, planning strategies in both areas remain fragmented and reactive. The paper calls for more integrated, circularity-oriented spatial planning that mobilizes skills and proximity as key territorial resources.

papers.title: From emissions to damage: A mechanism-based assessment of artificial intelligence's environmental cost and the limits of the sustainable energy transition
papers.authors: Ramez Abubakr Badeeb
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming the global economy, but its environmental impact presents a clear paradox, as it can improve efficiency while also increasing energy demand. Existing studies focus mainly on emissions, while policymakers care about the associated welfare losses. This paper shifts the analysis from emissions to carbon damage, capturing the monetized cost imposed on economies and societies. It also investigates and quantifies the mediating role of sustainable energy transition in the relationship between artificial intelligence and carbon damage. Using panel data from 37 OECD countries and employing instrumental variable two-step GMM estimation supported by three robustness checks, our results reveal three findings. First, AI significantly increases carbon damage, confirming that AI's scale and energy demand outweigh efficiency gains. Second, AI significantly promotes sustainable energy transition measured through a newly developed composite index capturing renewable deployment, energy access, and efficiency. This reveals the presence of a beneficial indirect channel. Third, the Sobel mediation analysis confirms that this channel offsets a limited share of AI's total carbon damage. Across our estimators, the implied mediation share remains below 15%, indicating that the self-correcting capacity of the sustainable energy transition is real but quantitatively limited. Moreover, a suppression mediation pattern is additionally identified, revealing that studies relying on total effect estimation without mediation decomposition underestimate AI's true direct environmental cost. This finding moves the debate beyond the question of whether AI is good or bad for the environment toward the more policy-relevant question of how much of AI's environmental cost the sustainable energy transition can absorb.

papers.title: Trade-offs between greenhouse gas mitigation and nutrient enrichment during tropical composting
papers.authors: Edwin Mwangi, Felix K. Ngetich, Collins Muimi Musafiri et al.
papers.abstract: Composting provides an opportunity to recycle organic residues into valuable soil amendments; however, amendment selection can create trade-offs between nutrient enrichment and greenhouse gas (GHG) mitigation. Our study evaluated the effects of different organic amendment combinations on GHG emissions and nutrient dynamics during tropical composting. Six cattle manure-based treatments were assessed: cattle manure alone (CM), cattle manure with Tithonia diversifolia (CMT), Tithonia with biochar (CMTB), Tithonia with citric acid (CMTCA), Tithonia with maize stover (CMTM), and Tithonia, maize stover, and citric acid (CMTMCA). We monitored composting for 84 days, measuring CO 2 , CH 4 , and N 2 O emissions alongside changes in temperature, moisture, pH, and carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus fractions. Greenhouse gas emissions concentrated during the thermophilic phase, the period of greatest emission intensity due to enhanced substrate availability, rapid carbon mineralization, and active microbial transformation. During this phase, cumulative CH 4 emissions ranged from 299 to 1284 g CH 4 –C m −2 , with CMTCA producing 180% higher emissions than CM, while cumulative CO 2 emissions ranged from 10.8 to 14.1 kg CO 2 –C m −2 , with CMTMCA and CMTCA producing 23% and 13% higher emissions than CM, respectively. CMTCA produced the greatest cumulative CH 4 emissions, exceeding CM by 165%. This response reflects the combined influence of Tithonia diversifolia and citric acid addition, where enhanced carbon solubilization increased substrate availability and microbial oxygen demand, potentially promoting transient anaerobic microsites favorable for methane production. Across the composting period, CMTM generated the highest cumulative CO 2 emissions, 18.5% higher than CM, reflecting enhanced carbon turnover from readily degradable substrates in Tithonia diversifolia and maize stover. Biochar amendment (CMTB) increased cumulative N 2 O emissions by 41% compared with CM, suggesting that biochar effects were dependent on interactions with nitrogen-rich Tithonia and compost nitrogen transformation pathways. Conversely, Tithonia-based amendments improved nitrogen enrichment but increased emission risks. Overall, the findings demonstrate that climate-smart composting requires balancing nutrient recovery and GHG mitigation rather than optimising either outcome in isolation. For smallholder farmers in tropical regions, the findings demonstrate that locally available organic amendments can improve compost nutrient characteristics. However, amendment selection should consider potential trade-offs between nutrient enrichment and greenhouse gas emissions.

papers.title: Synthetic textile upcycling to produce functional adsorbents: state-of-the-art, challenges and outlook
papers.authors: John Kwame Bediako, Mohammadamin Esmaeili, Godfred Ohemeng‐Boahen et al.
papers.abstract: The use of waste materials as low-cost adsorbents for treating water pollutants offers many advantages as they contribute to reducing waste disposal costs and aiding sustainable resource management. Synthetic textile wastes pose environmental threats, hence their upcycling to adsorbents for treating water pollutants presents a good option for sustainability and circularity. The synthetic textiles are employed in their pristine, chemically functionalized, or morphologically tailored forms, including fiber felts, electrospun membranes, 3D-printed monoliths, and activated carbon (AC). This review critically examined up-to-date research, common target pollutants, performance and trends regarding the upcycling of synthetic textiles to produce functional adsorbents for water treatment. Generally, adsorption performance towards organic and inorganic pollutants including emerging contaminants is controlled by surface area/porosity, surface functionality/chemistry, morphology, crystallinity, wettability, and stability. For metals and dyes, performance depends almost entirely on functionalization, e.g., coatings, grafting, carbonization. For hydrocarbons and oils, hydrophobic pristine textiles already perform well, however, performance is further improved via surface functionalization. For emerging contaminants such as microplastics and PFAS, synthetic textiles are largely underutilized, with current evidence dominated by microplastic-vector studies and composite materials rather than purpose-designed textile-based adsorbents. Noteworthily, the upcycled adsorbents serve potentially lower-cost and more circular alternatives in location-specific applications, rather than universal replacements for AC or ion exchange resins. Consequently, synthetic textile-derived adsorbents are economically promising, however, rigorous cost analysis, regeneration, real wastewater systems, and scale-up operations remain a major missing piece and a clear priority for future research. Additionally, comprehensive leaching and chemical screening are required prior to deployment. Moreover, spent adsorbents and regeneration liquors must be managed through metal recovery, eluate treatment, or controlled destruction, consistent with for example, EU textile collection and EPR policies. Standardized testing should quantify hydraulic performance, breakthrough behavior, dynamic capacity, mass transfer, mechanical stability, material shedding, bed utilization, and regeneration durability to enable reliable adsorbent comparisons.

papers.title: Spatio-temporal dynamics of migrating wet and dry extremes: structural coherence and land-use associations across India
papers.authors: Mayank Tyagi, Mohit Prakash Mohanty
papers.abstract: Abstract Global hydroclimatic extremes increasingly occur as cascading wet–dry sequences, challenging conventional single-hazard management. However, their spatiotemporal migration and associations with land-use patterns remain poorly understood. We present an integrated framework combining the standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index, a spatio-temporal density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise algorithm, and phase-wise land-use/land-cover (LULC) exposure analysis to characterize the migration, structural coherence, and persistence of major wet and dry extremes across India. Both dry and wet events exhibit a range of migration directions rather than a single dominant pathway, spanning northward, southward, and eastward trajectories. Although several recent events are among the least coherent, a linear-trend test does not establish a temporal shift towards fragmentation ( p = 0.74 for dry and p = 0.16 for wet events). A pronounced asymmetry between rapid onset and a prolonged recovery phase (2–3 months) highlights the persistence of hydroclimatic extremes. Phase-wise LULC analysis indicates that agricultural landscapes show the greatest absolute exposure, largely reflecting their extensive national footprint, while urban areas are frequently associated with recovery-stage wet events. The proposed framework provides a transferable approach for improving early-warning systems and supporting land-use-informed adaptation to compound hydroclimatic hazards.

papers.authors: Kareem Buyana
papers.abstract: Abstract Working with societal stakeholders is vital in addressing the adaptation limits and impacts of climate overshoots (exceeding the 1.5°C global warming limit). papers.title: Enhanced influence of the North Pacific Meridional Mode on the western North Pacific tropical cyclones in a warming climate
papers.authors: Liu, B., Jia, F., Gan, B., Cai, W. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Western North Pacific (WNP) tropical cyclone (TC) activity is strongly modulated by the North Pacific Meridional Mode (NPMM), yet how this influence responds to global warming remains unclear. Using observations and high-resolution atmosphere-only simulations that reproduce the observed NPMM-related environmental and TC responses, we investigate how warming alters the NPMM influence on TC genesis and tracks and the underlying physical mechanisms. We show that global warming strengthens and reshapes the NPMM-related TC response through an amplified tropical Pacific atmospheric response. Increased sensitivity of atmospheric convection to NPMM-related sea surface temperature anomalies enhances the convective response over the tropical central Pacific (CP), strengthening low-level cyclonic vorticity and increasing mid-tropospheric moisture over the southeastern WNP, thereby favoring TC genesis. Meanwhile, preferential strengthening of the southern portion of the NPMM-induced easterly steering flow directs TC activity and landfalls toward lower latitudes, producing a southward redistribution of NPMM-related TC tracks. Across simulations, stronger convective enhancement over the tropical CP is consistently associated with larger increases in TC genesis and lower-latitude track density. These results demonstrate that global warming can reshape regional TC risk not only by altering the mean climate state, but also by strengthening and spatially redistributing the influence of internal climate variability on TC genesis and subsequent movement.

papers.title: Biodiversity conservation and its associations with economic performance, inequality, and peace
papers.authors: Peereman, J., Orenstein, D., Chen, G., Lin, T.
papers.abstract: Abstract Biodiversity conservation is increasingly recognized as a product of coupled social–ecological systems shaped not only by ecological processes, but also by economic capacity, social inequality, and geopolitical stability. Here, we examined whether national conservation performance is systematically associated with economic prosperity, income inequality, peace, and the importance of natural resources in the national economy across 142 countries. Conservation performance was represented using the Nature Conservation Index (NCI), a composite metric integrating biodiversity threats, land management, governance capacity, and future environmental trends. We analyzed relationships between NCI, Gross National Income per capita, the Gini coefficient, the National Peace Index, and the total nature resources rents using a generalized additive model that accounted for nonlinear relationships and income stratification. Together, these societal variables explained deviance of 52.2% for the NCI model. Economic prosperity was positively associated with NCI, although the relationship was nonlinear across income groups, suggesting that conservation capacity does not increase uniformly with development. Counter to commonly assumed relationships between inequality and biodiversity loss, income inequality showed a positive multivariate association with NCI scores. This result suggests that high national conservation performance can coexist with unequal social conditions, potentially reflecting centralized or exclusionary conservation systems that elevate institutional conservation metrics without necessarily improving equitable biodiversity outcomes. We also found that more peaceful countries consistently exhibited higher conservation performance, supporting the view that geopolitical stability provides enabling conditions for sustained conservation governance and institutional continuity. We further suggest that national conservation indices may partly capture governance capacity, reporting infrastructure, and political commitment rather than ecological condition alone, while telecoupled trade systems may allow wealthier nations to externalize environmental pressures beyond their borders. Although the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, our findings highlight the need to interpret global conservation indicators cautiously and to incorporate social equity and externalized environmental impacts more explicitly into international biodiversity assessment frameworks.

papers.title: Higher prevalence of rising climate-driven snowmelt potential of rain-on-snow events in the Eastern continental US
papers.authors: Salvi, K., Ghosh, M., Kumar, M., Hao, D. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Rain-on-snow (ROS) events have significant hydro-geomorphological consequences. While these events have been widely studied, their meteorological capacity to thermodynamically alter or melt snow when unconstrained by snow amount, hereafter referred to as snowmelt potential (SMP), remains poorly understood, particularly with respect to its long-term trends. Here, we evaluate climate-driven trends in SMP, estimated as the snowmelt-inducing total surface energy flux transferred during ROS events assuming unlimited snow availability, across 8 991 sites in snow-affected regions of the continental United States over a 39-year period (1981–2019). Overall, SMP exhibits an increasing trend at ∼63% of the sites with the proportion of sites showing positive trends rising from 54.4% in the Western region, to 64.6% in the Central region, and 78.4% in the Northeastern United States. The spatial pattern of SMP trends remains robust to uncertainties arising from omitted radiative fluxes and dampened wind-speed trends. High-energy ROS events are found increasing at majority of stations, with the positive trends becoming more widespread as the energy threshold rises. SMP trends are primarily governed by changes in net radiation and sensible heat flux, modulated in large part by trends of event air temperature and wind speed. Findings suggest growing meteorological hazard potential from ROS events, especially at high-SMP sites, highlighting increased risk with continued climate warming.

papers.title: Decadal variability reveals contrasts in solar-resource stability across China
papers.authors: Meng, Y., Qiu, K., Wu, X., Wei, Z.
papers.abstract: Abstract Solar resource assessments traditionally focus on how much solar radiation is available and how it changes over time, while overlooking how stable that resource remains throughout the decades. Here, we quantify the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of decadal variability in downward surface solar radiation (DSSR), commonly known as global horizontal irradiance in the solar energy sector, across China’s seven major power grids during 1960–2024. We find pronounced regional contrasts in decadal DSSR variability, with the Central, Eastern, and Southern grids exhibiting greater variability, whereas the Western and Tibetan grids combine high solar resource abundance with comparatively low variability. The Central and Eastern grids also contribute disproportionately to national variability relative to their geographical area. By converting DSSR variability into indicative photovoltaic yield, we further illustrate that resource-driven yield uncertainty is substantially higher in the volatile eastern regions; however, spatial diversification across weakly correlated grids can reduce portfolio variability by up to 29%. These findings emphasize that the geography of solar-resource climatic stability differs from resource abundance, highlighting the critical need to incorporate decadal stability and spatial diversification into long-term renewable-energy and inter-regional transmission planning.

papers.title: Electricity retail pricing as incentives for load optimization in Vietnam
papers.authors: Doan, T., Portilla-Paveri, M., Lobos, N., Negrete-Pincetic, M.
papers.abstract: Abstract Vietnam’s pathway to net-zero emissions by 2050 has so far relied primarily on large-scale renewable energy investments, with limited use of demand-side management. This study evaluates how alternative retail electricity pricing schemes—flat tariffs, time-of-use (TOU), critical peak pricing (CPP), and a TOU–CPP hybrid—shape demand flexibility, system costs, emissions, consumer welfare, and reliability in Vietnam. The analysis uses SWITCH 2.0, an integrated capacity expansion and dispatch model with an iterative demand-response (DR) module, to Vietnam’s electricity system in 2050. Relative to flat pricing, the modeled TOU designs reduce total system costs by up to 15% and CO 2 emissions by 17.2%–37.5%, while increasing consumer welfare. Consecutive TOU blocks capture substantial benefits, whereas adding CPP produces little additional improvement. Endogenous block assignment achieves the lowest system cost and reduces storage investment, but does not yield the lowest emissions or highest consumer welfare. Sensitivity analysis confirms lower unit costs and emissions and higher consumer welfare under consecutive TOU than under matched flat-pricing cases across seven DR parameter combinations. However, the magnitude of these benefits depends strongly on the share of load available for within-day rescheduling. Demand shifting toward solar-rich hours also changes transmission utilization, relieving pressure on some corridors while increasing it elsewhere. The findings support a staged transition toward TOU pricing with simple consecutive blocks, accompanied by enabling technologies and coordinated transmission planning. The results represent conditional system-level outcomes rather than estimates of realized consumer responses or distributional effects.

papers.authors: Xinghui Tao, Zehao Ye, Guangming Wang et al.
papers.abstract: Segmenting segmental tunnel-lining point clouds supports automated inspection, but expert-tuned pipelines can degrade as conditions change. This paper presents R4Tun, a framework for bounded, deployment-label-free parameter adaptation of an expert-designed segmentation pipeline, guided by large language models (LLMs) using memory ( m ), state ( s ), and knowledge ( k ). On 30 selected Seg2Tunnel subsets (13 regular, 17 complex), three LLMs using full context increased mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) from 0.18 to 0.43–0.48 and overall accuracy from 0.42 to 0.59–0.65 over the static baseline. These results support R4Tun as a controlled, label-free, cross-LLM adaptation mechanism for the tested setting, with each parameter change auditable via logged rationales. Adaptation remains constrained by the pipeline’s fixed algorithms and design assumptions. R4Tun is therefore positioned as a mechanism-level contribution rather than a deployable inspection system.

papers.title: Public Risk Judgments of Endocrine‐Disrupting Chemicals: Psychometric Structure, Exposure Pathways, and Cross‐National Differences
papers.authors: Simonsen, N., Pravednikov, A., Lagerkvist, C., Perkovic, S.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Endocrine‐disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are pervasive in everyday life and pose well‐documented public health risks, yet little is known about how lay perceptions of EDC risks are structured and how they vary across exposure pathways and regulatory contexts. Drawing on the psychometric paradigm of risk perception, we conducted a large cross‐national survey () in Denmark, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Participants evaluated 18 EDC‐related exposure scenarios across nine canonical risk attributes, ranked perceived health risks by exposure pathway (consumption, inhalation, and dermal contact), and reported perceived severity, susceptibility, overall health risk, institutional trust, and sociodemographic characteristics. Across all three countries, risk perceptions exhibited a robust two‐dimensional structure corresponding to affective‐dread and cognitive‐deliberate dimensions. However, the relative salience of these dimensions varied systematically: cognitive‐deliberate cues accounted for more variance in Denmark, whereas affective‐dread cues were more prominent in the United Kingdom and the United States. Perceived risk also varied consistently by exposure pathway, with consumption judged the most risky, followed by inhalation and dermal contact, a hierarchy that showed minimal cross‐country variation. At the individual level, greater knowledge of EDCs consistently predicted higher perceived susceptibility, while gender, year of birth, income, parenthood, and institutional trust showed context‐ and outcome‐specific associations. By extending the psychometric paradigm to chronic, diffuse chemical hazards embedded in everyday activities, this study demonstrates that EDC risk perceptions reflect shared affective‐cognitive dimensions while remaining sensitive to exposure pathways and governance contexts, offering theoretically grounded insights for risk communication and policy design.

papers.title: From participation to data: collaborative mapping in the context of natural hazards and risks
papers.authors: Mara Remi, Marco La Salandra, Francesco Lovergine et al.
papers.abstract: Collaborative mapping has emerged as a key approach for collecting, analysing, and sharing geospatial information on natural hazards and risks. By integrating Citizen Science (CS) and Volunteered Geographic Information (VGI), it incorporates local knowledge, real-time observations, and crowdsourced data collection into risk assessment and management processes, where traditional data sources are limited or outdated. This study provides a systematic overview of collaborative mapping applications for natural hazards, including hydrogeomorphological (floods, landslides, coastal erosion), climate and weather related (storms and cyclones, wildfires, droughts and heat waves) and geophysical (earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions) as well as multi-hazards contexts, examining how different terminologies, actor types, and technological approaches are represented across the literature. A total of 105 peer-reviewed studies were selected following a screening process based on Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, starting from major scientific databases. The results highlight an uneven distribution of research efforts, with a focus on floods and multi-hazard contexts. Furthermore, collaborative mapping is predominantly applied in mitigation, preparedness, and response phases. In terms of technologies, while traditional GIS-based methods dominate, computational approaches like Machine Learning (ML) are gaining traction. These approaches increasingly rely on the combined use of complementary geospatial sources: satellite and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) imagery commonly serves as a basemap guiding the digitisation of features in OpenStreetMap (OSM), whose data are then extracted and integrated into hazard and risk analyses. This integration enables spatial datasets to be rapidly created and updated where authoritative data are scarce or outdated, thereby supporting disaster management across its different phases. By providing a structured synthesis of key elements, this review contributes to a better understanding of the current state of collaborative mapping in natural hazards and risks, identifies key gaps and directions for future research.

papers.title: Reuse of effluent from the paint industry for the production of Anadenanthera peregrina seedlings: A silvicultural and ecotoxicological study
papers.authors: Lidiane Brito de Sousa, Thainara Lima Araújo, Agostinho Cardoso Hlavanguane et al.
papers.abstract: Increasing water scarcity and the need for sustainable waste management have necessitated the reuse of industrial effluents, particularly when aligned with the specific characteristics of each industrial sector. Forest nurseries represent a promising setting for this practice, as their automated irrigation systems prevent the risk of over-application and reduce effluent mobility in the soil through deep percolation. This study evaluated the feasibility of reusing effluent generated by a paint-manufacturing facility in the production of red angico (Anadenanthera peregrina) seedlings. Plant growth and development and the ecotoxicological response associated with effluent application were analyzed. Two effluent concentrations (E50% and E100%) were tested, with well water as the control. Plant-free substrate irrigated with undiluted effluent (E100% without plant) was monitored to investigate the influence of plant presence on substrate characteristics. After 100 days of irrigation, seedling growth, Dickson Quality Index values, physicochemical changes in the substrate, and ecotoxicity assays using Eisenia fetida earthworms were evaluated. Notably, the effluent, particularly at a concentration of 100%, restricted early seedling development, reducing biomass accumulation and quality indices relative to the control and demonstrating clear phytotoxicity to A. peregrina. Therefore, although the effluent can aid fertigation, its application in the production of A. peregrina seedlings requires dilution to mitigate its phytotoxic effects. However, substrate analyses revealed that undiluted effluent increased microbial activity, as indicated by basal substrate respiration, and exerted an attractant effect on earthworms. These findings indicate that A. peregrina may contribute to the phytoremediation of soils contaminated with paint industry effluents.

papers.title: Balancing nutrients and metal contaminants: sustainable land application rates for livestock manures in Ireland
papers.authors: S. Farid, L. Morrison, M. Danaher et al.
papers.abstract: Livestock manures are valuable nutrient sources for crop production, but variable composition and inappropriate application rates can cause nutrient imbalance, phosphorus accumulation and trace-metal loading, increasing the risks to water quality and the wider environment. This study evaluated manure-specific application rates by considering nutrient and trace-metal composition, crop requirements and soil phosphorus status. It was applied to cattle, sheep and chicken manures used for perennial ryegrass ( Lolium perenne L.) and spring wheat ( Triticum aestivum L.) under Irish nutrient-management recommendations. Maximum application rates ranged from 0.96 to 7.62 t dry matter ha −1 yr −1 for perennial ryegrass and from 0.99 to 9.76 t dry matter ha −1 yr −1 for spring wheat across Morgan's soil phosphorus indices 1 to 3, representing increasing soil phosphorus status. No manure application was permitted at index 4. Cattle manure permitted the highest application rates because of lower total phosphorus concentration, whereas sheep manure supported the lowest. The governing nutrient constraint varied with manure composition, crop nutrient requirements and soil nutrient status, with phosphorus generally limiting cattle and sheep manure application, while nitrogen limited chicken manure application under specific conditions in TN-based calculations. Regulated trace-metal loadings remained below the annual permissible limits. Zinc and copper reached approximately 31% and 14% of their respective limits, while cadmium remained below 10% and chromium, nickel and lead below 2%. papers.title: Viewing extreme precipitation intensification through an absolute-change lens
papers.authors: Jiayi Ni, Changrui Zhu, Qun Yue et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract While relative fractional changes are widely used to characterize extreme precipitation intensification under climate warming, absolute changes provide a complementary perspective that more directly quantifies the magnitude of extreme precipitation intensification, with direct implications for assessing potential impacts. By analyzing annual maximum daily precipitation in climate models, we show that the geographical patterns of the strongest extreme precipitation intensification identified from absolute changes differ from those highlighted by relative changes, and that the most intense annual maxima exhibit substantially larger absolute increases than weaker annual maxima despite only modest differences in their relative changes. Although thermodynamic moistening produces broadly similar relative increases in stronger and weaker annual maxima, it leads to substantially larger absolute increases in stronger maxima, primarily owing to differences in climatological intensity. Dynamic contributions reinforce this intensity-dependent contrast in some regions, particularly in the South and East Asian monsoon regions and equatorial Africa. These contrasts highlight the value of considering absolute changes alongside relative changes to better characterize the magnitude and geographical patterns of extreme precipitation intensification and inform assessments of potential impacts under climate warming.

papers.authors: Estrada-Zuleta, J., Meneses Bernal, J., Avila-Diaz, A., Quesada, B.
papers.abstract: Abstract Climate-risk assessments in tropical wetlands increasingly combine hydroclimatic and land-cover data, but rarely integrate them with structured community evidence on experienced impacts and adaptation priorities. We address this gap in six communities around the Complejo Cenagoso de Zapatosa, a Ramsar site, and the Morales wetland in the Colombian Caribbean. We integrated hydroclimatic records and climate-extreme indices (1991–2020), land-cover change and runoff-potential analysis (1991–2020), flood-susceptibility modeling, and structured participatory evidence from 106 participants. Mean annual temperature increased by 0.4 °C decade −1 , while warm nights and warm days increased by 17.1% and 17.3% decade −1 , respectively; precipitation and precipitation-extreme indices showed no significant domain-mean trends. Forest cover declined by 1 122.9 km 2 , whereas flooded non-forest formations, agriculture/pasture mosaic, and oil palm increased by 800.9, 254.4, and 244.2 km 2 , respectively, altering runoff potential. Flood susceptibility was concentrated along floodplains and wetland margins (AUC = 0.95). Of 50 valid community-reported extreme-event records, 76.0% matched the expected sign of annual instrumental anomalies; both heat records matched, while agreement reached 91.3% for floods and 53.8% for droughts. Drought mismatches indicate that annual rainfall anomalies incompletely capture wetland drought, where dry-spell persistence, water-level change, and livelihood disruption shape local experience. Community priorities emphasized wetland restoration, hydrological connectivity, fisheries governance, livelihood diversification, and monitoring. Integrating technical and community evidence therefore revealed complementary climate-risk signals and the conditions under which ecosystem-based adaptation may be locally feasible.

papers.title: Influence of natural and anthropogenic forcings on western US winter fire weather and the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires
papers.authors: Srivastava, A., Risser, M., Ullrich, P., Wehner, M.
papers.abstract: Abstract Winter fire weather is shaped by interactions between anthropogenic climate change and natural climate variability, yet how the combination of human and natural forcings influences winter fire weather conditions remains poorly quantified. This study uses a multiple linear regression framework that removes long-term CO 2 -related trends to examine the influence of natural modes of variability on the December–February monthly fire weather index over the western United States (WUS), with the January 2025 Los Angeles (LA) fire risk as a motivating case study. Results show that the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), Pacific North American pattern (PNA) and Atlantic Meridional Mode (AMM) significantly influence winter fire weather across the WUS, whereas the influence of CO 2 is more pronounced and generally significant over the interior regions, but less evident along the coastal areas of the WUS. Positive phases of the PNA and AMM, combined with La Niña–like conditions during December 2024 and January 2025, significantly elevated fire weather risk across southern California, including LA County. The elevated fire-weather conditions preceding the January 2025 fires in LA and surrounding regions were aggravated by the combined influence of the natural and anthropogenic modes. Our study also shows that anthropogenic CO 2 is associated with an estimated 10%–20% increase in the chances of the 2024–25 fire weather over the WUS coastal states, although this contribution is not statistically significant, while La Niña and positive PNA significantly increase these chances by at least 20% across California and by more than twice across much of the WUS, including southern California and neighboring states. We find that large-scale natural climate modes combined with increases in greenhouse gas concentration provide valuable information for understanding and predicting WUS winter fire weather.

papers.title: Movement characteristics of persistent extreme precipitation events over China during the warm season using high spatiotemporal resolution data
papers.authors: Liu, K., Mao, J., Wang, X., Ren, J.
papers.abstract: Abstract Moving persistent extreme precipitation events (PEPEs) can cause severe disasters along their tracks. However, a PEPE typically consists of multiple rain cells that evolve and move differently from one another, rendering the conventional single-center tracking method incapable of capturing their respective characteristics. Here we use a multi-rain cell tracking method to characterize the movement of PEPEs during the warm season (May to September) over China, utilizing high-resolution precipitation data at half‐hourly temporal and 0.1° spatial resolutions for the period 1998–2024. Based on the movement distance and direction, PEPEs are clustered into the long-distance eastward-moving, short-distance eastward-moving, northeastward-moving, and westward-moving types, which are most prevalent over Southeast China, the Tibetan Plateau (TP), Northeast China, and the southern China, respectively. Temporally, the frequency of these four types of events peaks progressively from May to August, and the PEPEs with longer movement distances tend to occur in the early morning. In terms of large-scale circulation patterns, long-distance eastward-moving PEPEs are favored by the southwestward extension of the Western Pacific Subtropical High (WPSH); short-distance eastward-moving PEPEs are associated with a meridional dipole of geopotential height anomaly around the TP; the northeastward-moving type is likely influenced by a wave-train circulation pattern in high latitudes; westward-moving PEPEs occur more frequently when the WPSH extends northwestward. These findings provide a comprehensive climatology of PEPE movement and highlight distinct circulation controls, which may aid in the prediction of moving extreme precipitations.
